Header: Aonidiella aurantii, Lepidosaphes beckii, Chrysomphalus aonidum

Prevention: Avoid the use of broad spectrum insecticides, as these will kill natural predators of armoured scales and cause higher infestations of the pest on citrus.
These insect pests can spread rapidly as they are highly mobile.
Wear protective clothing/ check clothing when leaving a citrus plot and before entering a pest-free area to avoid spreading scales.
Purchase certified nursery stock to prevent initial infestation.
Reduce local ant populations which protect scales from natural enemies (via planting of repellant plants such as mint or cinnamon).
Monitoring: Observe citrus trees every week, look for presence of scale insects on 5-10 random twigs per tree.
For red scale ( A.aurantii ), check five random fruit per tree.
Small (2 mm long), circular insects, commonly reddish-brown, shaped like a mussel shell.
Symptoms of armoured scale infestations are:
Yellowing of leaves which may drop prematurely.
Poor growth of infested plant due to heavy feeding.
Sticky honeydew on the stem and leaves, may be covered in black sooty mould.
Commonly associated with ant presence due to their feeding on honeydew and protection of scale insect from natural enemies.
Sample at least 20 trees per acre.
If insect pest is found in high populations (when 10-15% of sampled trees are infested) then undertake direct control measures.
Direct Control: Use of parasitic wasps such as
Metaphycus luteolus, M.stanleyi, M.helvolus or the parasites
Aphytis lignanensis in tropical regions and
A.melinus in temperate conditions (release roughly 300 000 per
Ha, consider advice from local extension officers).
Use of insecticidal soap (5 teaspoons of bleach-free washing liquid per litre of water).
Spray every 7 days until infestation has cleared.
Use of oil spray (2 tablespoons of cooking oil and 2 tablespoons of soap with 1 gallon of water).
